name: Guanajuato
summary_text: Guanajuato is one of the country's sharpest contrasts: among the most lethal states and one of the most advanced legislatures. It recorded the second-highest state count in the 2021 national report of violent deaths of LGBT+ people (9, in a year led by another state with 10), and has remained among the top states in subsequent years. It was simultaneously the first state in the country to pass a comprehensive sexual-and-gender-diversity law - approved unanimously by all 32 deputies across the governing and opposition parties on 15 February 2024 and published 7 June 2024 - and it amended its penal code the same year to add sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics. But Human Rights Watch devoted a March 2024 documentary to discrimination against trans people in Guanajuato over identity documents, and a federal court had to order the state congress in June 2024 to create a rights-respecting recognition procedure - the statute book moved faster than the administration that must apply it.

sources.title: Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time; the underlying Human Rights Watch news feature (31 March 2025) reviews progress and remaining challenges for trans rights in Mexico - state-level gender-recognition reform, pending legislation and violence/impunity - the country-level frame against which each state's deviation is scored.

sources.title: “I Just Want to Contribute to Society”: The Need for Legal Gender Recognition in Tabasco, Mexico | HRW
sources.claim_summary: Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024): documents how the absence of any legal gender-recognition procedure in Tabasco exposes trans people to police stops, denial of documents and institutional mistreatment - the country's clearest case of administrative erasure, cited to establish what a state without any procedure does to trans residents and visitors.

sources.title: Transfemicide becomes a crime in a ‘watershed’ moment for Mexico City | Transgender | The Guardian
sources.claim_summary: The Guardian global-development report (24 July 2024): Mexico City criminalised transfeminicide with sentences up to 70 years after the 2016 killing of trans sex worker Paola Buenrostro whose attacker was released despite footage and witnesses and remains at large; activists call the law a watershed in one of Latin America's deadliest countries for trans people, while the reporting notes convictions lag the statute - the benchmark for judging other states' transfeminicide laws.
